utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Everyone. One small update, we've identified a translation error that occurred with a Witness RM322 on May 28th. It was Exhibit P01500, 65 ter 04032. We've uploaded a revised English translation under ID 00822150 ET/1 and have informed the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber requests, then, the court officer to replace the original translation with the revised one and the Defence has an opportunity to revisit it. I've got no idea what the document is, Mr. McCloskey, but if you would be so kind to tell the Defence where the change is found, then it may save them quite some time in trying to locate the error.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Ms. Stewart will be able to do that quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to deal with a -- with a Rule 94 bis filing for Witness Brown. The Chamber has granted last week a Prosecution request to reclassify as confidential certain annexes of the Rule 94 bis filing for Witness Brown. Due to the format of the filing, the Registry is instructed to redistribute the entire filing as confidential and the Prosecution is invited to file a public redacted version thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps needless to say but nevertheless, you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey will now continue his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 6289.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, good morning. We are on 13 July and the -- going over some of the materials you studied in your capacity as the intelligence analyst for the Srebrenica team. And this is from a now-familiar person, Ljubisa Borovcanin and it is one of his -- a report to the Minister of Interior, Ministry of Interior Special Police Brigade, as we see 13 July. Again I won't go all over all of it but if we could look at that first page in English and we see the description of the units that went into Potocari across Zuti Most in the early morning hours and took control of Potocari at 1300 hours, and took control of the Budak and Milacevici features?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, sorry for interrupting, you said at the beginning the report to the minister and then Ministry of the Interior Special Police Brigade. I only see this term on top of that page. That seems to be the institution from which this letter was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct. I apologise. We see that it's to the Pale police staff and the other two people listed there. That is the heading. Thank you for that clarification -- that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the -- that first paragraph, does that comport with your understanding of the events from other documents and videos and other materials you've studied?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it says: "In Potocari, we sealed off the main UN base where a throng of between 25.000 and 30.000 civilians had gathered." Again, is that number within the rough estimates that you have seen repeatedly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about this approximately 5 per cent of whom were able-bodied men? 5 per cent of 25.000, what do you make of that figure, based on your understandings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it appears to be roughly in line with other documents that I've seen, which corresponds to somewhere north of a thousand, maybe up to 2.000, individuals who are ultimately separated at Potocari, I believe there are some VRS reports that indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I won't do the math on the percentages but we can do that. And we see that the -- it notes that the MUP forces was involved in the organisation of the evacuation of the civilians, and did you see that on the video that you studied?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the next page in English, we -- it speaks of combat on the night between the 12th and 13th and a loss of -- "the enemy sustained a loss of 200 soldiers who were killed and we captured or had surrendered to us around 1500 Muslim soldiers and the number increases by the hour." Can you tell us very briefly what are you -- what do you know about any potential combat where the Muslims lost significant numbers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. On the evening of 12 July 1995, and through the early morning, the dark hours of 13 July 1995, the portion of the column that was still south of the Konjevic Polje-Nova Kasaba road again attempted to cross over the road to join the portion of the column that had made it across the night before. By and large, they were not successful in being able to cross the road, small elements of them did get through, but by that time, the Bosnian Serb military, as well as police forces, had been able to gather in that area in enough strength to prevent the full remnant of the column from successfully crossing the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this notice that they had captured or surrendered 1500 Muslims and it was increasing by the hour, what day do you take this increasing by the hour to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be on 13 July 1995, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this -- if we recall going through the after-action report from yesterday, was this number mentioned in it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. When one looks at Colonel Borovcanin's after-action report that was published in September 1995, there is no mention to the fact that his forces at any time held prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you make anything of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By September of 1995, clearly Colonel Borovcanin would believe that it is in his interest not to be mentioning the fact that his units had prisoners. Certainly by then not only did all of the VRS with respect to Eastern Bosnia have a fairly good idea of exactly happened and why but by then even the international community was levelling allegations and in some cases showing documentation or aerial images that highlighted the broad-scale massacres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And finally in that last paragraph, it says: "Muslim soldiers who did not manage to break through is on the rise and is approximately between 5.000 and 6.000." How does this relate to what you were just telling us about that -- that combat and the inability of many -- many Muslims not to get across the road?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It corresponds to that and there will be other military documents, for example, coming from the Bratunac Brigade or the other military unit there, the 5th Engineer Battalion, that I believe offer similar number estimates as to those remaining in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer that document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06289 receives number P2117, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2117 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 4051 now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we are waiting, we'll see this is a -- what is now -- should be a familiar, the reports that Dragomir Vasic, the chief of the centre, police centre for Zvornik, is sending out. This is dated 13 July and it talks about a meeting in the morning with General Mladic where: "We were informed that the VRS was continuing operations towards Zepa and leaving all other work to the MUP as follows. "Evacuation of the remaining civilian population from Srebrenica to Kladanj, about 15.000." Talks about needing petrol. Is -- does this information comport with the other documents and material you've seen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the next line, it says: "Killing of about 8.000 Muslim soldiers whom we blocked in the woods near Konjevic Polje, fighting is going on, this job is being done solely by MUP units." What do you think this reference to killing of about 8.000 Muslims who were blocked and then with the additional sentence, "fighting is going on"? How do you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I rise -- the B/C/S original does not say "killing." It says "liquidation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we seek confirmation there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll agree with that. That's well known and it's -- "liquidation" is always a tricky word to translate. In fact it could be done as "liquidating" but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's -- we see that "likvidacija" is the word used there, and may I take it that it is a point of dispute on what that means between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm note sure there is, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then there is not. That's good. Now, has the word "likvidacija" been verified as being properly translated in "killing" or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In my view, it depends on the context of the way it's used. We've seen it used in the context of combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mainly my question is has it been verified? I mean if CLSS has considered that in this context this is the right translation, then I would just like to know whether attention has been paid to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, this term has been used and, for years, with no issues, so as many of these things, they are self verified for years because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Self verification is not something I -- Mr. Ivetic, do you challenge the translation into "killing" or do you draw our attention to the fact that this translation may depend on circumstantial considerations?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that "liquidation" in a military sense has a specific meaning and that is not the same as "killing" so I dispute the translation as being an accurate translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then has it ever been verified by CLSS?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't recall any -- any resubmission of this by anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then since there is a challenge, I leave it to Mr. Ivetic whether or not he wants to submit it for verification. Our attention has been drawn to the issue. The original says "likvidacija," the translation before us now is "killing." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Butler, in looking at that, in the term that's used that you're evaluating, what kind of killing do you interpret that to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I went through the same issue when I first saw the particular context of this word and obviously I am aware that there is a more sinister English connotation than in fact I've been told by various translators that exist in the word in Serbo-Croatian. In this particular context, I take this language to mean that they are going to continue the job of killing in a military sense, a military attack on the remnants of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you view this as a report on continuing combat? Is that similar to what Mr. Borovcanin mentioned in the previous document, that we have combat ahead of us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Or Borovcanin and Vasic in your view talking about the same group of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean they're both up and down that road on 13 July so both individuals have an opportunity to gain information from the various police units, particularly that are along the road, so the fact that they would have a common picture of what they understood the military situation looked like for the remnants of the column that were trapped in that area on 13 July 1995 is not surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is our view of the context of this so I don't know if that solves the problem but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not my problem at this moment. It was Mr. Ivetic's problem. I think I've been clear if he considers that it needs to be further verified, he can ask for that and otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was my understanding. That's my understanding and I will comply with that, Your Honours, and get that fixed. My concern is, of course, when someone sees the document apart from the transcript it could lead to different conclusions. For clarity I think I will submit it and I'll report back once that is done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, was there -- was there fighting with these thousands or by the end of the 13th, what does -- what do the documents show as we'll soon get to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. What the documents show not only on the 13th but also on the 14th, 15th, 16th, through the 17th and 18th, that the army and the police units that are surrounding the column are still engaged and conducting military operations against it through at least the 18th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And by the end of the 13th, how many of these thousands actually surrendered along that road, from the documents and intercepts you've reviewed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents, the intercepted communications of the various members of the VRS and police on the road, as well as images from a source known as the video along that road that was done by Minister Petrovic, reflects that somewhere between 2.000 and 3.000 individuals from the column probably surrendered on that day and are assembled in various places along the road. And as we go further in through some of the documents and some of the information, some of these correspondents will give numbers of the estimates of these individuals that they have captured and where they are located at various points in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll go over that. You have over the years provided estimates of roughly what your view of how many people may have been killed in the woods in possible combat from the area of Buljim all the way up to Baljkovica. What rough estimates have you provided?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of the column or at least how I look at the column is kind of in part why I explained the estimates that I've given. My early understanding of the composition of the column and of the battle casualties result of it in the early part of the investigation are between 1.000 and 2.000 individuals, I believe, killed in combat with the VRS from the origin of the column through Baljkovica. Now, I've not in detail analysed the military activities of the column with respect to the various ambushes that it's been involved in, nor have I really looked at the issue of the column and tried to parse through casualties for other reasons. I think that's impossible to do and I certainly didn't attempt to do it. For me, the issue of the column was only germane for two particular reasons. The first reason was, from an analytical and military perspective alone for my analysis, whether or not the column was a military object subject to attack or not and I've concluded that it was and I understand that there is another school of thought out there on the subject. The second issue that I care about analytically of the column is being able to retrace the column's route during various days and at various times so that when there is issues related to military activity primarily by the Zvornik Infantry Brigade on the days of the mass executions, I am able to distinguish between that military activity that was involved in what I considered to be legitimate combat operations against the column and that military activity that was not engaged against the column and correspondingly was used to support the mass executions that were occurring in the zone of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade from the 14th through the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection with the caveat that I will send to CLSS but I think it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04051 receives number P2118, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2118 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we now see 65 ter 4036.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another -- a document from 13 July, with the heading of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to the commands of the Drina Corps and several brigades, entitled, "Order to prevent the passage of Muslim groups towards Tuzla and Kladanj." And again I won't go over this in detail. But I do want to note on the second page that it's from assistant commander Lieutenant General Milan Gvero, and it's talking about the column and referring to them, saying: "Among them are inveterate criminals and villains who will stop at nothing just to avoid being captured and reach Muslim-controlled territory." It goes on to talk about: "Detain the captured and disarmed Muslims in appropriate facilities," that's in paragraph 3 under the order, "that can be secured by fewer troops, and immediately report to the superior command." And at the second page in the English as we can see it says: "Send interim reports with specific details of the situation in the area of responsibility of all units so that the corps command and the Main Staff can act in a timely manner." Briefly, Mr. Butler, how is it that General Gvero in your view is getting involved in this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As we are aware, with respect to where people are, at this point in time, General Mladic is still in the Srebrenica-Bratunac area. General Tolimir is down in Zepa. I believe General Miletic is still present at the Main Staff but certainly so is General Gvero, and so the fact that as a general and as a senior officer of the Main Staff, the fact that he would put out an order like this under his own name to the Drina Corps and various units for this information, is not surprising. Again, one of the basic bedrock foundations when one looks at these various documents that I ascribe to is the fact that the VRS is a professional army, these individuals, many of these generals have 20, 30 years of experience as well as a significant amount of professional education and that in the context of the issuing of military orders and documents, they are not going to issue orders and documents that they know that they are not authorised to issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04036 receives number P2119, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. May I ask one additional question on this document? On the second page, there seems to be quite some attention to the use of secure channels of communication, about the captured or blocked groups. Is that common in an order, to emphasise the necessity of the use of secure channels, or is it exceptional that you specifically pay attention to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe it's exceptional, sir. The army of the Republika Srpska obviously was aware that their communications or much of their communications were subject to intercept. One of the secure forms that he would be talking about is that while they had some encryption devices, sending these types of message via radio telegraph was considered to be one of the more secure forms of communication because it could not be readily intercepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I see that what is everyone was expected to do. My question was more about emphasising it again in an order where it should perhaps be routine to use secure channels. So my question is how common is it to specifically pay attention to it in an order like this one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I take your point, given that it should have been a routine issue, on the 13th of July, 1995, the VRS was capturing and gaining custody of thousands of individuals which was not a routine situation for it. It had never obviously captured that many people on a single day. The idea that keeping at least your adversary, the 2nd Corps ABiH, keeping them in the dark about how many people are actually being captured, as well as what the actual military situation involved on the ground is something that they would want to achieve. So the 2nd Corps people don't know what's going on to that extent. So it is a routine thing to do to not talk about prisoners or not talk about people you capture or not talk about military operations, but there was nothing routine about the fact that they were capturing so many people and that may have prompted General Gvero to feel he needed to reiterate this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, it's P1255.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an intercept that the Trial Chamber has seen. And therefore I don't want to have to spend too much time with it, Mr. Butler, but we can see that it's the 13th of July and that the -- at 1015 hours, and the participants are Beara, Lucic, Zoka - and this should be confidential - and do you -- who do you take Beara and Lucic to be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beara is Colonel Beara, the head of the VRS security office. I believe the investigation has identified Lucic as Lieutenant Lucic, the assistant commander for intelligence and security of the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see Beara is speaking on this and he says: "Do you hear me? Do you know that 400 balijas have shown up in Konjevic Polje?" They talk a bit about that, disarmed. And it says, he goes on at the bottom of the page to say: "Shove them on the -- all on the playground, who gives a fuck about them." This use of this term, Mr. Butler, is this an example of what you were referring to about senior officers using derogatory terms towards the enemy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I discussed this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it goes on to say on the next page of the English: "Well, line up -- line them up in four to five rows." So where do you take -- who are these -- what's he referring to and where do you take this to mean, these people are being put?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Military Police Platoon -- I'm sorry Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment is garrisoned in Nova Kasaba. In this particular context, the people that he's referring to are individuals, the Bosnian Muslims who are being captured as a result of the column attempting to cross the road, and the location that they are talking about putting them on the playground is in fact putting them on the soccer pitch that is in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as part of your investigation, did you review aerial imagery of that pitch?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have seen an aerial image of that pitch on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it consistent with this information on this intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Beara, in the various other intercepts that you've reviewed, some of which we'll be going over, and references and documents, very briefly, what was he involved in during the days of 13, 14, 15, 16, from your analysis of those intercepts and documents, but just very briefly, not in detail?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Beara, with respect to the broader crime base, is a central figure. He is -- on the 13th he is noted very deeply involved with issues related to getting counts of prisoners. On the 14th, 15th and 16th, the military documents and the intercepts have him up in the Zvornik Brigade area where much of his activities also correspond to the executions of the prisoners that are being held in schools in the Zvornik Brigade area. So he is a central figure, a key central figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in any of the materials that you've read, have you found any indication that he was involved in proper counter-intelligence work, which we've heard should be 80 per cent of his job, or the 20 per cent military legal work? Any legitimate work that you see Colonel Beara involved in from any of the documents or references?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously in his respect in -- his defence was he was doing just that, so as a result of my responsibilities as the team military analyst obviously it is an issue that I looked into very heavily to see if we -- there was any information that could corroborate that. All of his activities had to do with the criminal actions related to the prisoners. We were not able to substantiate that any of the activity that he was performing with respect to dealing with the prisoners was any activity that could correspond to his counter-intelligence responsibilities of his functions as the chief of security for the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, P1558.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we'll see this is a document from the IKM of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment and at the top, it says: "Borike at 1400 hours." Can you tell us -- and if we go to the second page in English we'll see what -- it's Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic. First of all, tell us who Savcic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic at the time was the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure we have -- this is the right document up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This one seems to be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we go back to the -- we now see that that's Savcic and you've told us who he is and we see that it's the time it was dated. Now, what is Borike?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borike was a forward command post associated with the Zepa operation. I believe it was the command post of the -- the forward command post of the Rogatica Brigade, and they used this also as a command post with respect to their ongoing first negotiations and later military attack at least as far as the Rogatica Brigade was, on Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see that it's entitled "Procedure for treatment of war prisoners" and it's to the commander of the Main Staff for his information. And then it says assistant commander for morale, religious, legal affairs of the Main Staff. You've identified that as General Gvero, for his information, and to the commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment order. Who -- remind us who is the commander of the 65th Protection Regiment -- excuse me, the Military Police Battalion of the 65th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Military Police Battalion is Major Zoran Malinic, so in this particular sense, Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic is his immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see that it starts out with: "There are over 1.000 members of the former 28th Division of the so-called BiH army captured in the area of Dusanovo, Kasaba, prisoners are under control of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment." Is that information consistent with what you learned, that there were a thousand prisoners in Kasaba at about this time on that date?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where do you think they are in Kasaba based on this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my understanding is that most of the prisoners were being assembled on the open soccer pitch. It was one of the few places where they had enough space for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The next line is: "Assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the Main Staff proposes the following measures." And this title, who is this a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the Army of the Republika Srpska is General Major Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it says -- so Tolimir proposes -- well, to paraphrase, Tolimir proposes the following measures. What does -- this indication that he's proposing something, does this tell you anything about what -- where -- what Savcic is doing and where Tolimir may be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And again I've testified about this particular document before. My understanding of this document is that at the time that this document is drafted, General Tolimir is together with Colonel Savcic and that this is actually a two part document depending on whether it is addressed to you for information purposes or whether it is addressed to you as to take as an order. The first two points are proposals by General Tolimir to the broader Main Staff suggesting security and other proposals that should be taken as a result of what is happening. When you look at points 3 and 4, you can see that they are not proposals, they are in fact orders, and they are orders specifically to the Military Police Battalion, which falls under the command of Colonel Savcic. So again, while it is a combined document, on one hand Colonel Savcic is in writing putting down the proposals based off of his knowledge of what they are from General Tolimir, and in the other part of it he's giving orders to his subordinate formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can see that the first two proposals have to do with secure -- secrecy and securing those -- the two roadway areas. And does that -- do those areas described there, does that include the -- where the prisoners are being assembled at the soccer pitch in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That would include -- I mean obviously it would include part of the soccer pitch because that's where the 65th Military Police Battalion is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And getting to point 3: "Commander of the Military Police Battalion shall take measures to remove war prisoners from the main Milici-Zvornik road, place them somewhere indoors or in an area protected from sighting from the ground or the air." Who had access to the air, to day-time flights at this time in the war, as far as you know, in this area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS was well aware that NATO was conducting, was flying over Bosnian air space to include the Republika Srpska, and is aware that there was aerial reconnaissance being done, not only by aircraft but by unmanned aerial vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your view, at 1400 hours, was the -- had murder operation orders been issued?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And does this order to place people indoors or in an area protected from sighting from the ground or the air in your view have any relation to that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I've given the opinion that it does. As the Court will be aware, particularly on the 13 July, during the day-time hours, the VRS was still moving busloads of individuals from Potocari along the road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Milici out towards Kladanj, so also going along those roads would be various UN personnel that could still get out of Potocari and had not been taken into the custody of the VRS or had their vehicles confiscated. So there was a concern, as noted here, to both hide the numbers of prisoners who were taken from aerial observation as well as to place them in positions where they could not be viewed from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And going to the next page in English, we see that it says: "Once the commander of the Military Police Battalion receives this order, he shall contact General Miletic and receive from him additional orders." Where do we get Miletic involved here? How does this fit in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again General Miletic is the chief of operations for the VRS Main Staff. The closing of major road networks, for whatever reason, General Tolimir felt that that was beyond his authority to direct. The proposal in part sent to General Gvero at the Main Staff obviously would be shared with General Miletic of the Main Staff but ultimately it would be the decision of General Miletic as the chief of operations whether these roads would be closed. In light of the fact that these proposals have been made, it's not unsurprising that Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic, being engaged in other things at the time, would instruct his subordinate commander to directly contact another unit or in this case, the Main Staff, in order to verify that the proposal had been accepted or to get additional instructions in the event that the proposal was modified somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So on that point, right at the end, it says verify if the proposal has been approved by the commander of the VRS. And I take it you're saying these first two points, is that the proposal that is being referred to in paragraph 4 in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was Mladic -- did you find any -- any information or documents to indicate whether they were able to verify with the commander, Mladic, on this point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware if General Miletic coordinated directly with General Mladic on this point or not. What I am aware of is that apparently the proposals were accepted because there will be supplemental orders issued that in effect does close those roads to most civilian traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to look at the document. The name is not coming to me off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, which is 65 ter number 5700.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll see this is -- has the top from the -- top marking Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, it's 13 July, and we can see if we look at the Serbian version, it's from General Mladic with an SR next to it, which, in speaking with Mr. Ivetic, we can agree that the SR term, I believe -- and he pronounces it better than I do and in the proper tense so if he could say that, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Svojom Rukom [Interpretation] In his own hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see on this there is a translation into "signature" on the original. Our translator said in the courtroom if you've -- we've all heard, "in his own hand." I'm fine with either of them. The Main Staff officers may have a better idea of which one is more appropriate. Again a context issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, is this one of the documents you were talking about just now, where you said that we would see if the proposals were followed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see that this is from General Mladic. We can see that it's entitled, "Preventing leakage of military secrets in the area of combat operations, order." And then we can see: In order to ensure the organised conduct of planned combat operations, mentions Srebrenica, and then we see the various closures and notices and other references on this topic. If we look at the bottom of the English page, number 5, it says, ban on giving information. And then it goes on, particularly on prisoners of war, evacuated civilians, escapees and similar. We don't see any order about putting people indoors or outside the air but do you connect this document at all with the proposal from General Tolimir issued in Savcic's name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, when one looks at the road closures and in general, the fact that -- prevent giving them information about the announcements, it's clear that General Mladic has at least been briefed about the broad outlines of General Tolimir's proposals and this is -- accepted them, modified or amplified some as he felt necessary and is issuing this as an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05700 receives number P2200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now could we have P1280?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I doubt if this is the correct number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, P2120, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2120 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And P1280 should be not shown. It's an intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Butler, you'll see that this is an intercept from the 2nd Corps, from 1602 hours, and in looking at the context of this intercept, do you know what date it's talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it's X and Y and it mentions where Malinic unit is, they said that there are 1500 gathered at the stadium. So this is a couple hours later than the document related to the thousand people. Is this the same area that you were talking about before, the stadium where Malinic unit is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's Malinic unit, the 65th Protection Regiment military police group?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it in fact says that in the last line where it -- and it says: "We probably won't let any get by."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next intercept which should also not be shown. P1281.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Another 2nd Corps intercept at 1730 hours, between X and Y. And you had mentioned there would be materials where numbers of estimates and prisoners were given by the VRS. Is this one of those materials that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had testified that you'd thought there were 2.000 to 3.000. We now see from this: "Well, tell them right away to come. There is about 6.000 of them." What do you think this 6.000 is referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be the correspondent's estimates of how many prisoners that they already had in their custody along a large stretch of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know this is a reference to prisoners and not something else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as one looks down, again, first, when one looks at 13 July, this is a 13 July 1995 intercept, when you look at the body of this particular intercept, it discusses that they have them at various locations along three points. Other documents and intercepts as well as the investigation are able to corroborate that at three different points there were large groups of prisoners being held by the VRS on 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Remind us of those three points?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was the soccer field at Nova Kasaba, football pitch. Another one was at the intersection at Konjevic Polje. And the third one was where they were assembling many of them on the meadow of Sandici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we've just seen documents and intercepts about the soccer field that up to 1500 that afternoon. If we go to Sandici and Kravica, what are the rough estimates from the video and the documents and the exhumations from Sandici and Kravica for that grouping?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I try to remain conservative, and again I'd look at it as there is probably about a thousand prisoners at each location, for a total of 3.000, I would say. Obviously, there was not an accurate headcount done by anybody so the fact that the numbers are all off the board, either up or down, is not surprising. So when we always talk about the numbers of prisoners that are being captured, they are in generalities but certainly they number in the thousands and not the hundreds or not even the tens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another intercept, P01615. I see it's -- I believe it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for a break. Could we ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we go to P1064?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going out of chronology for a moment, Mr. Butler. I believe this is a document you've spoken to, about, before. If we could -- we'll look at it, that it's from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade dated 8 August 1995, to the command of the Drina Corps. It's a daily combat report and we can see from the next page it's from the commander of that brigade, Rajko Kusic, and it is briefly in the days August 8th, were those the days after the Zepa enclave had fallen and there were Muslim men and boys fleeing in the woods?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this, we see the term liquidated, which I wanted to see if we can get a better handle on that term. We see on 7 August 1995, in the afternoon, in the canyon of the Praca river, five remaining balijas who were after the fall of Zepa travelling along the following route. And it gives a detailed route. Crossed the Drina River on logs. Another route. Went down the railroad tracks at Dub and tried to reach Renovica walking on the railroad tracks were liquidated. And there is some Serbian term that sounds like that being used in the original. The group was separate and travelled for 10 days. The same day in the vicinity of Luke, an unarmed Ustasha born on the 24th -- excuse me, born in Srebrenica, 24 years old, was liquidated. Do you, in the context of these people being killed, do you find that there is anything related to combat in this account of these people being liquidated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, what do you find this to be -- what is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the absence of any indication of combat activities taking place would lead to the inference that these people were killed after capture, because they were able to at least get some information from one of the persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So this is of course a different context than the 8.000 being liquidated that Vasic mentions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's get back on track. That's already in evidence. Let's go to P1786. And this is a Drina Corps command report and I very briefly it's a regular combat report, the first page we see a reference, the enemy in the former Srebrenica enclave is in total disarray. One group, 200 to 300 enemy soldiers managed to cross over into the Udrc section or sector. And we see this is under the commander Major General Krstic. Is this 200 to 300 correct or is this what you've been referring to as bad intel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As intervening days go on or actually in this particular case, as the day of the 13th and through the 14th go on, it becomes clear that the number of soldiers who got across the road or at least the VRS estimates of the numbers of soldiers is greatly off and that, in fact, the number does not number in the hundreds, several thousand managed to make it over the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to P1290.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an intercept and this should be confidential. And participants Badem, remind us what Badem is the code name for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Badem is the telephonic code name for the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Deronjic, who do you think Deronjic is, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic is -- at this point in time he's been appointed the civilian commissioner for Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do we have the document on the screen already? Are you on 290?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't, Your Honour, I -- 1290.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is a kind of technical problem. It's still loading somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for that. I'll try to keep my eye on that. And we can use the -- we can revive ELMO, if he's still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's wait for a second to do that. Until we know more about what to expect. Perhaps we should revive ELMO for an exceptionally -- because the nature of the problem is uncertain, as is the time it will take to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me -- perhaps I could ask Mr. Butler to give up his copies because mine have a -- some highlighting and other items on it. But I don't mind if Mr. Ivetic has my secret highlightings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I actually have it up in e-court, I thought. I was able to get it on mine. If it's 00912585 is the ERN?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I think e-court is functioning privately but not -- I am working on e-court at the moment as well and it functions for me also. But -- could it be put on the ELMO, Mr. Usher? I think we can see it now, isn't it? We can continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, just go back into time and if you can see this, we see that it's an intercept, you've mentioned who -- I believe you've mentioned who Deronjic is. We see it mentions Karadzic's intermediary and then in parentheses the intercept operators has written down the intermediary and Karadzic are sitting in the same room. This is at 2010 hours. Do you know the date of this intercept from your review of all the materials?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this would be 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see a discussion where Badem says: "Hello, I have Deronjic on the line." And then Badem, the person from the -- which would be the person from the Bratunac Brigade, correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Says: "Deronjic, speak up." Deronjic says: "Hello, yes, I can hear you." Then Badem says: "Deronjic, the president is asking how many thousands." Deronjic says: "About 2 for the time being." What do you think Deronjic is referring to in this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Miroslav Deronjic is referring to the number of prisoners that by his calculation are being stored in facilities in and around the town of Bratunac on the evening of 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And Badem then says: "2, Mr. President." Deronjic says: "But there will be more during the night." What do you take that to mean? That there will be more during the night?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Mr. Deronjic is aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a practical problem on the Defence side. Mr. Lukic, in order to follow the ELMO, the other button has to be pushed. For me it's the right, top button out of six. The problem then is that we only see the English. Mr. McCloskey, that requires that at least everything relevant or if you have an original then perhaps it could be provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I do. Ignore the highlighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, it's your highlighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler has unhighlighted versions and so he can provide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if you have an original, then, yes, I do understand we can't have them both on the screen. If you would give your copy on a temporary basis to the Defence, then they could give it to Mr. Mladic. Yes. We work on the basis of the English but the B/C/S version is by courtesy of Mr. Butler available to Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where we left off was right there in the middle of the English. When Deronjic says: "But there'll be more during the night." Based on your analysis of all the evidence, what do you think that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic is aware that even at that time, on 13 July 1995, the various military and Special Police units that are along the road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Nova Kasaba, are still capturing prisoners as well as moving hundreds more from these locations for the evening to other locations closer to Bratunac where they could be more securely guarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then Deronjic says: "Do you want me to come down there to Cerska where are you calling from?" Can you make any sense out of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, Cerska is a region in Eastern Bosnia. He's not physically present there. I believe that the investigation has determined that Cerska was the telephonic code name used for President Mladic's office or at least the facility he was talking to at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Talking about code names, is there any dispute about that, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is dispute, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if I may just.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be -- let's try to remain organised. Apparently Mr. Mladic is seeking to consult with Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic, your client apparently seeks to consult with you. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, that might assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm drawn -- my attention is drawn to the fact that the witness stated President Mladic and that this was President Mladic so I believe he might be talking about someone else. I'm told that Cerska was never the call sign for General Mladic's office nor was he ever in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's the position of the Defence. I do understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, if I said President Mladic, obviously I mean President Karadzic, a sure sign that I've not had enough coffee yet this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so it was -- you referred to President Karadzic and not to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On that issue the investigation cannot currently confirm Cerska, so just to update us on that. That -- I should say as a code name of some sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was waiting for because Cerska as an area I take it is confirmed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that Deronjic says: "Can you hear me, Mr. President?" "The president can't hear you, Deronjic." This is the intermediary. Deronjic says: "I have about 2.000 here by now." Then a teleprinter drowns him out apparently. And then X says: "Deronjic, the president says all the goods must be placed inside the warehouses before 12 tomorrow." Then Deronjic says: "Right." And X says: "Deronjic, not in warehouses but somewhere else." Couldn't make out what was right in there. Mr. Butler, what do you think X is referring to when he says -- the president says in quotes: "All the goods must be placed inside the warehouses before 12 tomorrow"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is talking about the prisoners, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that last, second-to-last line, "not in the warehouses but somewhere else," what, if anything, can you make of that vague reference?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In context, one obviously must remember that there is still a considerable international presence in Bratunac on 12 and 13 July, between not only UNPROFOR forces but there is also members of MSF and other elements of the international community who have been lobbying very hard over the past several days to be able to gain access to the refugees and to individuals following the fall of Srebrenica in order to deliver humanitarian supplies and things of that nature. So clearly, there is concern here that they don't want these people in locations where they might be viewed by members of the international community transiting through Bratunac. So the idea of getting them out of Bratunac as quickly as possible is something that we see occurring starting on the evening of the 13th, going on through the 14th, 15th and 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: E-court is functioning again, so therefore we don't need the ELMO any further, and could the copy which was given to the Defence be returned to Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to be clear, Mr. Butler, that analysis, was that based solely on these words on this intercept or are you basing it on other knowledge from the investigation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Again, when I offer a conclusion of this nature, I have to do so understanding the broader context of what is happening at the time in order to -- for it to make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did the investigation reveal Muslims were taken that night of the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting the evening of the 13th of July, 1995, what the investigation has revealed is that the first bus convoys of Bosnian Muslim men who had been separated at Potocari and who were in the hangar facility in Bratunac were transported under escort to the school in Orahovac in the Zvornik Brigade zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to a document we have marked as 65 ter 04205. And this is portions of the Bratunac military police log which I know we have seen before, but I would like to go to page 12 in the English and page 15 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: E-court broke down again. Therefore, if you have a hard copy, we could still use the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We had both that and Mr. Butler has, and I have -- I actually have unmarked copies of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would provide the unmarked copies, if you would give them to the usher, the usher may then give them to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I just need the B/C/S. I have the English, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that's B/C/S also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and we have two B/C/Ss, if -- two Serbians, if need be for the general and his -- and Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then could it be provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we use the ELMO again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What page, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 12 in the English and this is 11 July, for the Serbian. And we just -- I just wanted to ask you, we do see a reference that the MP squad secured the Spat-Pribicevac road for passes for General Mladic and others. This is on the 11th. Do you relate this to what you testified previously?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us where?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, with respect to the location of General Mladic in and around the Bratunac-Srebrenica area on these corresponding dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page, it's page 13 in the English. It's July 12th and 13th in the Serbian. Mr. Butler used to operate the ELMO so I think he knows how to do that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in the days when dinosaurs ruled the planet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if looking at this reference to 12th and 13th of July, it says the police were engaged in securing UNHCR. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you sure that's not supposed to be something else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no, you're correct. In this particular context, what they're -- what the military police in Bratunac are doing is securing UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, all right. And we can see the rest of what it says. And it's night duty at Fontana and the UNHCR school securing the commander Ratko Mladic. What do you take that securing Mladic to mean at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just essentially what it reflects is the fact that obviously the general of the army is a high-value target for the enemy, and that he is somebody who would require additional security in order to ensure his personal protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this give you an indication of where he may have spent the night?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe this, and there are other records available, that shows that he spent the night at -- in Bratunac, the evening of 12th and 13th July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's jump ahead of our chronology a bit and go to the next page, on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although e-court is functioning again, the system seems not to be stable at this moment so therefore, if -- for the time being could -- continue as we do now and then perhaps after the break, everything will be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if you could put 14 -- it should be page 14 in the English and it's the 14th, 15th of July listing in the Serbian. The police was engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees. Now, this is the 14th and 15th. Are there any Muslim women and children still left in the Potocari-Bratunac area on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What in your view is this a reference to, then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, this is a reference to the activities of the Bratunac Brigade military police who were escorting convoys of the military-age men from detention facilities in and around Bratunac to the school locations in the Zvornik Brigade area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall the names of the military police commander in Bratunac that was involved in that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a number of years. I believe if I recall correctly, the last name of the military police platoon commander was Mr. Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is, I take it, different than Radoslav Jankovic of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They are different individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And was -- does the information show who the commander of the Bratunac Military Police Platoon was working under the direction of that day in this job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously the platoon or the military police platoon commander is always under the command of the brigade commander. However, there is a great deal of information that reflects that he is working in concert with and for Colonel Beara and Colonel Popovic with respect to organising the transportation of individuals from -- or from -- the military-age men from Bratunac to the facilities in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's now jump to the 17th, it should be page 16 in the English and of course it's noted as the 17th in the Serbian. And it's that second to the last line, I want to call your attention to, it says, one police patrol remained in Pilica to secure and guard the Muslims. What is -- in your belief, is that a reference to and what do you base your opinion on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As the investigation has shown, one of the primary detention facilities in the Zvornik Brigade area that was used was the, we call it the school at Kula in the broader Pilica area and obviously the investigation has been able to document that over a thousand individuals were detained at that facility. This reference, again, this puts the Bratunac Brigade military police up away from the Bratunac zone and in fact puts elements of them in the Zvornik Brigade zone dealing with these individuals. The only Muslims that are in Pilica are those that have been brought there by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But on the 17th of July, are you aware of any alive -- any living Muslim prisoners in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. At this point, they've all been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One more date. Let's go up to the -- should be page 22. It's the date of 23/24 July. I'm not sure you got a copy of that. It's a relatively new addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it should be page 22 in the English and page 25 in the B/C/S on e-court, if that's working. Yes. That's it. Not yet there in the Serbian. Got the Serbian, got rid of the English. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This reference: Six Muslims in detention were brought in the course of the day, two more Muslims were brought later but they were sent back because they cut their own throats with a bottle while they were in detention in Skelani. They lost a lot of blood and they were sent back. Do you recall any reference to anything similar to this from the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook? Do you recall this, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Despite the ability of the VRS to apprehend thousands of these individuals, one of the things that has been documented by the investigation has been that there were Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica who successfully managed to evade capture and, in fact, went to Serbia, at that point over the Drina River, it was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. One of the things again noted in the investigation also is that on occasion, members of the Serbian MUP would turn these people, once they were captured in the FRY, they would make arrangements and then give them back to the military police or other authorities of the army of the Republika Srpska and there are nations of that both within the Bratunac Brigade military police taking custody of some of them as well as the Zvornik Brigade taking custody of some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember the specific incident about the people that cut their own throats? If you don't we can go forward.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall bits and pieces of it, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we may get to that later. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that the B/C/S is, I believe, 200-some pages and the English is 22. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This maybe needs some organisation, I acknowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then reserve a number already so that it is easily spotted in the context of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll fix this. Most of it's already in D30 -- D285. We just added those last two pages, so we will either sort it on to the D exhibit or make -- but we'll work that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, it's good for the transcript that we know -- we have now the D number and most likely it will then be added to the D number so that those who are reading the transcript know where to find it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll get that done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then no need to reserve a number for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, back to the 13th and some of the more significant documents, let's go to 65 ter 4118. And this is a document that, and the heading is from the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade known as the Rogatica Brigade. To the VRS, to General Gvero personally, entitled, "Accommodation of RZs," which is -- means prisoners of war. And it's from General Tolimir. And we can see that it says: "If you're unable to find adequate accomodation for all the RZs from Srebrenica we hereby inform you that space has been arranged for 800 prisoners of war in the 1st PLPBR in Semac [phoen]." There is an unknown word that we have been told meant some kind of military bed in later years. "The 1st PLPBR can guard them with its own forces and would use them for agricultural work, maintaining the horse, pig and sheep farm. If you send them to the sector this must be done at night using 1st PLPBR transport and troops. It would be best if this is a new group which has not been in contact with the other RZs." Now, you've already told us that General Tolimir was over in the Rogatica area. Is he still there at the writing of this, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that it was -- up in the right it's handwritten submitted 2230 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we have, as you can see, Mr. President, if you see -- and others, the typewritten original in the Serbian and then what is on the back is a handwritten draft of the same, is what we have been always informed. Both of which you can see on the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you think this is a reference to, what does it tell us about General Tolimir's knowledge of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, having testified against -- about this document previously, the first thing that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, could you just wait for a minute?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please, if you could continue. I'm sorry for that. This is an important document.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Given the time that this document was drafted and sent, the evening of 13 July 1995, it has been my conclusion at this point that not only does General Tolimir at this juncture know that there are thousands of prisoners being taken and that they are being moved from the Bratunac area, he is also aware that the plan is now to kill the prisoners. The investigation has looked into the facility that General Tolimir has proposed to use and it is determined at the time that it did not contain horse, pig, sheep or livestock of that nature. It was a relatively abandoned facility. And I also believe that looking at both the military documents and as well as other investigative activities that the team has done, the Rogatica Brigade was not equipped or prepared or did not have the logistical ability to support approximately 800 prisoners of war for a long-term duration. So that if prisoners were being sent to that facility, there was no way to take care of them for very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you factor in that this is personally to General Gvero, if you do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, at this point in time, I believe that General Gvero was also into the knowledge of what the plan is with respect to executing these individuals. He's sending it to General Gvero at the Main Staff because that is where he wants this to go. He could theoretically send it to Bratunac. He could theoretically send it to Vlasenica. He knows that General Mladic is moving from location to location, but also as part of the larger plan, he knows that at sometime on the 13th he expects General Mladic to be back at Han Pijesak at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As far as you know, has the investigation revealed any indication that prisoners were actually sent towards Rogatica in this direction?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04118 receives number P2121, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we are at last into 14 July, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter 08491.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document with a heading of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. And it's from General Mladic, as we see, the Serbian, we see no SR next to it. And we do see in the English on the second page some indications of received 14 July at 0800 hours. Now, as we look at this - I won't read it - we see that it's a -- it's a document to all those listed, and it's talking about the failure of the power supply at Veliki Zep which the Trial Chamber has heard about is a key comms area and just notes that: All information that you have for exchange with the Main Staff of the VRS should be prepared and exchanged during operating hours of the centre. How do you view this document, is this something that General Mladic would have been aware of? His name is on it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the sense that, I mean, clearly this is a routine document. General Mladic would have been aware of it in a broader sense. Again, going back to my discussion about military officers who are members of the Main Staff who would be issuing orders in General Mladic's name within their competence to do so, the -- an order like this, it's not necessarily that General Mladic would have hand drafted the order, but certainly given the gravity of the communications network being down for a certain period of time, he would have been aware of it and it would have been an appropriate order to issue under his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 08491 receives number P2122, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
