utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should also decide that P2122 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could go to P01298, which is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is an intercept - this should be confidential - from the 14th of July between General Mladic and an unidentified person X. I won't read it all. We see it's a friendly conversation. And then General Mladic in the middle of it says -- well, he's asked at the end: "Are you going to be there these days?" And General Mladic says: "Well, I am after Sunday." And then the person says: "But not today and tomorrow?" Mladic says: "I'm busy but I am today, if you can come over." K says: "You'll be there late in the afternoon?" Mladic says: "Until 1500 hours and then I'm going to the field. I'll be busy for two or three days and then I'm coming back."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, the Defence -- we have spoken briefly about this, and have agreed that the calendar of 14 July was a Friday; 15th, Saturday; the 16th is a Sunday. Just to help in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, does this help with identifying General Mladic's whereabouts when you relate it to other evidence in the case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this juncture, the general is at his headquarters. Obviously, as both the investigation and the historical record note, at some juncture on 14 July 1995, he travels from there and goes to Belgrade, and this is -- conversation is a reflection of a discussion, I mean, General Mladic does not go to the field. He does in fact go to Belgrade and he is there the evening of the 14th through the day of the 15th. I'm not exactly sure at what point on the 16th he returns to the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document. This is P363, and Mr. Butler, we are now in a -- taking a brief look at some notes that were retrieved from the Mladic residence well after your time period in the investigation, but have you had a chance to look at those notes that you have been told were taken down by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just intervene for one second? I do understand that part of the problems in uploading - I think it's the document you are now asking for again - is that the limit for documents in e-court is that it should not be bigger than 5 MB, which stands for megabytes, and the OTP is therefore invited to resize the document and put it back to e-court. That is what may have caused the problems but I see that Ms. Stewart is disagreeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's not about the same document. It was about P1290 which caused earlier the problems, but it doesn't affect, if I have understood everything well, the present document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think we are back together. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Butler, as you've just referenced that during your time there was evidence of meetings, and since that time, have you had a chance to look at these short notes of General Mladic's for those days?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I've been able to look at the portion of what I understand to be his notes for the various day periods here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see at this meeting, it's 14 July, 2115 hours, with President Milosevic and Bildt and General de La Presle. And there is a note President Milosevic explained the situation around Srebrenica. And then we -- I won't read all that out but we can see that it has to do with the ICRC, UNHCR convoys, about Srebrenica and Zepa. And then B is about convoys and supplies. Can you remind us who Bildt is, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a member of what is broadly referred to as the Contact Group, one of a number of political representatives from the international community seeking to broker a peace agreement to end the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go -- it should be B/C/S page 3 as well as English page 3. And under Bildt's heading, General Mladic has written down: To accomplish something over the weekend or we are going to get ourselves into trouble. I won't ask you about that. But then it says: Srebrenica, to free the boys, young men who were taken to Bratunac. What in your view is that a reference to, based on your knowledge of what was going on in Bratunac at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated in my previous testimony on what was happening with respect to Bratunac and who was there, the UN, the UNPROFOR forces that were in and around Srebrenica and many of them who were -- had travelled through Bratunac escorting convoys, clearly had an awareness that military-age men had been separated and were being held in and around the areas of Bratunac. One assumes at this juncture that the UN people in reporting these developments back to their higher headquarters, that at some juncture word of this got to and Mr. Bildt was made aware of this fact. The fact that General Mladic would have written this notation down in his notebook leads me to infer that it was an issue of discussion and that there was an awareness between Mr. Bildt and General Mladic that there were men who had been taken to Bratunac from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you find, as a military person, General Mladic's presence and work that he's clearly doing at this meeting, do you find that to be in any way an exercise of command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He's commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. Everything that he does or everything that he does not do as the commander is an exercise of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if he's at a wedding enjoying himself, that wouldn't be an exercise of command, would it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There obviously will be certain select circumstances where his presence at a personal event or his presence -- or even, for example, as a result of injury or illness he is not able to exercise command, and under the normal military procedure, if he cannot exercise command, arrangements are made for his deputy to assume command. In this particular context, where he's meeting with the president of a separate country, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and is meeting with members of the international community, and other military officers, his military assistant, I don't think one could categorise this particular meeting as a personal or social visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is it? Briefly, in military terms, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, looking at the larger context of what was occurring politically at the time - and I may not be the best witness to testify related to this - the Contact Group was very actively involved in seeking an end to the war in the former Yugoslavia, and one of their strategies was to meet directly with President Mladic -- I'm sorry, with General Mladic, excluding President Karadzic from those discussions because at that time they believed that General Mladic was the more reasonable party and they were hoping that General Mladic could be made to accept ideas with respect to a way to successfully conclude the conflict. So these meetings, while they did not occur presumably with the knowledge of President Karadzic, would certainly fall within his competence as the commander of the Army of the Republika Srpska to represent his army interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile I take the opportunity, Mr. McCloskey, you have shown to the witness P1558, that was about clearing the roads, partly being order, et cetera. And then you showed -- next you showed to him another document which is now admitted as P2120 and when I looked at it, it seemed to be quite familiar. Now, it is a different version although literally the same text as P1559, different stamps, different printing, but from the text exactly the same. That is the document where the Main Staff of the army, through Mr. Mladic, his name is at the bottom, reiterates more or less the cutting off the roads, et cetera. So just to assist everyone, that's P2120 and P1559 are similar in content. We take a break and we'll resume at quarter past 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I want to stay on this one page briefly. We see that the -- that General Mladic appears to have written: Liberation of Dutch soldiers, to free at least 48 or 86 Dutch soldiers who are with us. And I think you referred to that previously, those are the Dutch soldiers being held in and around Bratunac at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall with -- General Smith was at the meeting on the 14th or did he come after?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that General Smith's meetings with General Mladic were on the 15th, not the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 5791.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a -- one of those teletypes we can see with the Main Staff, the Army of Republika Srpska. It's to the Drina Corps, to the commander personally, the 1st Bratunac Brigade, for your information. And it's in the name of General Mladic with SR. And it says: "Pursuant to a request by the commander of the Dutch Battalion and in order to organise and facilitate an honourable sendoff for a group of about 50 members of the Dutch Battalion from Bratunac to Ljubovija, I hereby," and then we see it talks about enabling Dutch Battalion, about 50, who spent the last days in Bratunac to leave Bratunac. And take some of them personal stuff with them. Do you relate that at all to what we just read in Mladic's notes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And again, the fact that, you know, going back to your previous question, whether or not General Mladic is still exercising the facets of command as the leader of the VRS, at this meeting and subsequent to it, this again shows that he's not operating obviously in a personal capacity. He's operating in his capacity as the Commander-in-Chief, I'm sorry, as the commander of the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when his notes say, "liberation of Dutch soldiers," and then to free at least 48 or 86 Dutch soldiers, this document basically is doing that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this, we see that its headline is the Main Staff. If General Mladic is in Belgrade at the time, is there anything unusual about a document going out with SR at the bottom in his name, with the titles from the Main Staff or -- that we see here. Doesn't actually say from the Main Staff but we know what that means, this Main Staff header up in the left side.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, in this context, I could -- I could speculate a number of ways by which the order of General Mladic made it from Belgrade to the Main Staff. Suffice to say, the fact is that General Mladic's order with respect to what would be done did make it to the Main Staff, and was sent out from the Main Staff to the Drina Corps and the Bratunac Brigade as it was his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see a little handwritten note up in the right-hand corner, it says: Follow up on implementation of this order. And then someone initialled it. And this was obtained from the Drina Corps collection. What does that indicate to you, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's addressed to the Drina Corps command, commander personally, and it notes the fact that they are following up on this order. I mean obviously the people who received this order are taking it exactly as what it is. It's a lawfully issued order by their superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you -- have you been able to follow up to see if this actually happened? Did -- on the 15th, is there any indication that Dutch soldiers went out on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think over the course of several days later, I don't -- I'm not sure if it starts as early as the 15th, it may, but certainly over the course of the coming days Dutch soldiers begin to be released and sent into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would object based upon the notation "SR" meaning "by his own hand," as this document could not have been authored by General Mladic subsequent to the meeting as is being indicated in his own hand, that is to say, personally writing out. It's logically not congruent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it to say that this is a forgery, that this is not an authentic document, not received by those who signed for reception and not having been in the hands of those who made notes on it? Or is it that you say that there is something wrong in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It could can be either. At this stage we don't know. We're just making an objection based upon that to the admission of the document, pending our further investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I may reply to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may but if you give us one second, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, if you would respond to the objection to admission, and if you also could inform the Chamber where the document was found, as we have it here. And Mr. Mladic is -- can consult but should do it inaudible. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That -- this appeared to me to be an argument more of a weight to the document as to the admissibility, but of course, Your Honours would like, and expect, as you should, some form of foundation for it, and as you know, there are so many documents we have not individually done that or we would still be here. This, in my understanding, is what we got from the Drina Corps collection, which you've heard about before. In other cases we have taken the time to have Tomas Blaszczyk talk about that in detail, where it came from. It's a rather unique situation. And we have not done that yet, though Mr. Blaszczyk is always on stand-by ready to respond to any legitimate Defence concerns about that, and we can do that. We'll need more time, of course, but I can tell you as an officer of the court it's the Drina Corps collection and it's been used and testified about many, many times now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you assist me, that's the archives of the Drina Corps which contained this document, where it comes from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and just to give you the heads-up on that, that was a collection that was found in Serbia at a military base, and the RS police notified us of its location and they were able to arrange bringing it to Bosnia where they provided it, the RS police provided us boxes of original documents to a British base, and that's the subject matter of Mr. Blaszczyk's testimony. And many, many documents that we have introduced here that you see originals of come from that collection and he can testify about that, about how valuable or -- not how valuable but does this -- how credible it is, how credible a collection it is based on our review with other documents from other collections. And it's been quite a bit of work in that area, though we -- it's used so much by the Defence as much as it is us, the collection itself is not usually challenged, though we can, of course, understand why an individual document may get challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything to add, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, only that we have objected to the Drina Corps collection as a whole. That does not mean that certain documents from the collection might not be authentic. But as a whole, given the fact that it was -- the manner which it was collected and there is other details there in terms of whether it remained in the custody of the officials the entire time I know were discussed in other hearings and I had prepared to cross-examine Mr. Blaszczyk when he originally was scheduled to testify, thinking that that was the subject matter that he was going to testify about. So we would maintain our objection to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you again assist me? You said you objected to the Drina Corps collection as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. That's between counsel and I when we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's not in the -- not before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considered the arguments by the parties. The objection is denied. The document is admitted. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05791 receives number P2123, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2123 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 5419.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The very similar-looking document, same date, under the name of General Mladic SR. And this one we see it's to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Drina Corps, to the commanders, and it's ordering, making orders, we can see, to ensure the General Smith team is able to travel on 15 July. We can see that that's through Bosnia and further to Belgrade. And gives the details of when it's happening and making sure he has escorts. And, Mr. Butler, do you view this document as an exercise of command by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do we see indications of General Smith actually making it to the meeting in Belgrade on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in your view, was this order carried out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, same objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told we have the same objection to this document, Your Honours, as with the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And nothing further to add, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Nothing further to add, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe we have the originals, if that makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear that Mr. Ivetic is concerned about the originals not being there, so that's -- the objection is denied, similarly to the denial of the previous one. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05419 receives number P2124, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2124 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can now go back to P363, page 4 in both languages, back to the -- General Mladic's notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This, as you'll see, is noted as the 15th of July, 1995, the meeting with the UN and Milosevic, as he notes in his own hand. And as we get there, we'll see that he notes down people as Stoltenberg, Akashi, Bildt, de La Presle, General Smith. So, Mr. Butler, we now see Smith there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that the same Smith that was the subject of the last order that we saw by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of another General Smith who would hold that position or be meeting with General Mladic. I take it that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And under the note, "de La Presle," we see: "Liberation of 48 Dutch men is taken care of." Is that related in any way to the order about Dutch men that we just saw, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Going to the next page in English, we see notes about the ICRC wanting to meet with the prisoners, UNHCR reference. And General Smith says -- tells General Mladic that he will use force when the UN forces come under attack. And he notes that General Smith tells him there are rumours of atrocities. In your view, is General Mladic exercising and in command and acting as the commander of the VRS Main Staff at this time when he's taking these notes and engaged in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's now get to 15 July, 65 ter 1927. We have another order in General Mladic's name, with an SR. It's to the command of the East Bosnia Corps and the IKM of the Main Staff, for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see that he apparently is sending a comms sergeant to General Milovanovic over in the Krajina. Is -- and it's got "SR" on it. Is -- in your view does this indicate he is exercising command at this time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would again object based upon the date; the location of the General - as agreed by the parties - on the 15th; and the fact that the document purports that it was written by his own hand, which it could not have been done from that location. And so we would object to the -- to the authenticity of this document as one being authored by General Mladic personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the document, the authenticity of the document, is not the same issue as whether he signed the -- originally. It may be that someone made a mistake or that someone put an untruth -- an untrue statement in a document, but that is not about authenticity, even if there is an agreement about the whereabouts of Mr. Mladic at that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. And I believe that this document also comes from the Drina Corps collection - counsel can correct me if I'm wrong - and we have questions about the manner in which that was maintained, so for someone to have perhaps fabricated the document is not beyond the realm of possibility. We are investigating this, and at this time we have to object to the document based upon our concerns that are raised as to whether this document was actually issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is denied as well. Perhaps no need to say, Mr. Ivetic, that if your further investigations reveal anything which is relevant and which might cause the Chamber to reconsider its decision on admission, then of course we would like to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, that's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, the document is admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 01927 receives number P2125, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2125 is admitted into evidence. And you may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, I thought you had dealt with this, but I may be mistaken. Is it in a military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Mladic lower the volume of his voice in such a way that if there is any need to consult that it doesn't interrupt the examination of the witness. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can an order such as this be drafted upon the oral orders of General Mladic, where he orders that "SR" be put next to the type-set name so people understand he is personally involved with it? I thought you had testified about that already, whether the person had signed it or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. It wouldn't -- if it comes to pass that this was an oral order initially passed over the phone and the individual at the Main Staff who typed up this order, he's receiving the order directly from General Mladic in that sense, that it wouldn't surprise me to find that he would put "SR" because he had received the order directly from General Mladic. These -- none of these represent anything that I view as an abnormal command or staff process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just ask, Mr. Butler, when a document -- we have seen documents here which say "Mr. Mladic" and there is no "SR" next to the name but there is also no signature, how do -- that we see on the documents that are here - and I understand that currently there are originals elsewhere - are you able to comment on the difference between one such document where there is no "SR" but there is no signature and one where there is an "SR" and there is no signature? What is the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, as evidenced with the documents that are -- that have been sent through various radio digital transmission means, you're not going to get a physical signature on the document. There are occasions that I have seen copies of documents where an original version may be signed but copies of that document are not signed, sometimes simply for lack of carbon paper or an obvious lack of a Xerox machine to make multiple copies. Again, when I look at these particular documents, I look at them in the broader context of the professional military command and staff processes, and that individuals who are, by their profession and by their position on the Main Staff, are accorded certain authorities to issue orders, sometimes in the name of the commander, if they are in a certain competence that has been previously defined, and that much of my analysis of the military documents comes from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will later find out whether it's a drill or whether it's serious. We leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 6th day of September, 2013, at 9.30 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.46 p.m.,
